blocks.p: When they had agreed on this much, they wrote another letter to Diabolus and sent it by the hand of Mr. Profane. These were its contents:
The lords of Looseness, from our dens, caves, holes, and strongholds in and around the wall of the town of Mansoul, send greetings to the great and high Diabolus:

Our great lord, and the nourisher of our lives, Diabolus: how glad we were to hear of your fatherhood’s readiness to help forward our design to ruin Mansoul, no one can tell except those who, as we do, set themselves against every appearance of good whenever and wherever we find it.

As for the encouragement your greatness is pleased to give us to keep devising, contriving, and studying the utter ruin of Mansoul, we need no urging there; for we know very well that it cannot fail to be pleasing and profitable to us to see our enemies, and those who seek our lives, die at our feet or run from us. So we are still contriving, to the best of our cunning, to make this work as easy as possible for your lordships and for ourselves.

First, we have considered that most hellishly cunning, close-knit, threefold project which you put to us in your last letter. We have concluded that, though blowing them up with the gunpowder of pride would do well, and tempting them to be loose and vain will help things along, yet contriving to bring them into the gulf of despair will, we think, do best of all. Now we, who are at your beck and call, have thought of two ways of doing this. First, we for our part will make them as vile as we can; and then you, together with us, at an appointed time, will be ready to fall on them with the utmost force. And of all the nations that come at your whistle, we think an army of Doubters may be the most likely to attack and overcome Mansoul. So we will overcome these enemies; or else the pit will open her mouth on them, and despair will thrust them down into it.

To bring about this design we so much desire, we have already sent three of our trusty Diabolonians among them, disguised in dress and with changed names, and the townspeople have taken them in: namely, Covetousness, Lasciviousness, and Anger. Covetousness has changed his name to Prudent-thrifty, and Mr. Mind has hired him, and is now almost as bad as our friend. Lasciviousness has changed his name to Harmless-mirth, and has become the Lord Willbewill’s footman; and he has made his master very wanton. Anger changed his name to Good-zeal and was taken in by Mr. Godly-Fear; but the peevish old gentleman took offense and turned our companion out of his house. In fact, he has told us since that he ran away from him, or else his old master would have hanged him for his pains.

Now these have done much to help forward our work and design on Mansoul; for in spite of the spite and quarrelsome temper of the old gentleman last mentioned, the other two are plying their business well, and are likely to ripen the work quickly.

Our next proposal is that it be settled that you come on the town on a market day, when they are in the heat of their business; for then, to be sure, they will feel most secure, and least expect an assault to be made on them. At such a time they will also be less able to defend themselves, and to hinder you in carrying out our design. And we, your trusty (and, we are sure, your beloved) ones, will be ready, when you make your furious assault from outside, to back up the business from inside. So in all likelihood we will be able to throw Mansoul into utter confusion, and swallow them up before they can come to their senses. If your serpentine heads, most subtle dragons, and our highly esteemed lords can find a better way than this, let us know your minds quickly.
To the monsters of the infernal cave, from the house of Mr. Mischief in Mansoul, by the hand of Mr. Profane.

All the while these raging renegades and hellish Diabolonians were plotting its ruin, the poor town of Mansoul itself was in a sad and woeful state. Partly it was because they had so grievously offended Shaddai and his Son; partly because their enemies had gained fresh strength within them through it; and partly because, though they had pleaded by many petitions to the Prince Emmanuel, and through him to his Father Shaddai, for their pardon and favor, so far they had not won a single smile. On the contrary, through the craft and cunning of the Diabolonians in their own households, their cloud was made to grow blacker and blacker, and their Emmanuel to stand further and further off.

The sickness, too, still raged fiercely in Mansoul, among the captains as well as the townspeople; and only their enemies were lively and strong now, and likely to become the head, while Mansoul was made the tail.
By this time Mr. Profane had carried the Diabolonians’ letter to Diabolus in the black den, going by way of Hell-Gate Hill as before, and passing it through Cerberus to his lord.
But when Cerberus and Mr. Profane met, they were at once as thick as thieves, and so they fell into talk about Mansoul and the project against her.
“Ah, old friend!” said Cerberus. “Are you back at Hell-Gate Hill again? By St. Mary, I am glad to see you!”
“Yes, my lord, I have come again about the affairs of the town of Mansoul.”
“Tell me, then, what condition is that town of Mansoul in at present?”

“In a fine condition, my lord, for us, and for my lords, the lords of this place,” said Profane. “They have fallen far off from godliness, and that is as good as our hearts could wish. Their Lord is badly out with them, and that pleases us well too. We have a foot in their dish already, for our Diabolonian friends are lying in their very bosoms; and what more do we lack but to be masters of the place? Besides, our trusty friends in Mansoul are plotting every day to betray it to the lords of this town; the sickness rages bitterly among them; and to crown it all, we hope to prevail at last.”

Then said the dog of Hell-Gate, “There is no time like this to assault them. I hope the enterprise is followed up closely, and the success we want is soon achieved. Yes, I hope so for the sake of the poor Diabolonians, who live in constant fear for their lives in that traitorous town of Mansoul.”

“The plot is almost finished,” said Profane. “The lords in Mansoul who are Diabolonians are at it day and night, and the others are like silly doves; they lack the heart to concern themselves with their own state and to see that ruin is at hand. Besides, you may, indeed you must, conclude, when you put everything together, that there are many reasons pressing Diabolus to make all the haste he can.”

“You have said it as it is,” said Cerberus. “I am glad things have come to this. Go in, my brave Profane, to my lords; they will give you as lively a coranto, a capering dance of welcome, as this whole kingdom can afford. I have sent your letter in already.”

Then Mr. Profane went into the den, and his lord Diabolus met him and greeted him: “Welcome, my trusty servant. Your letter has made me glad.” The rest of the lords of the pit greeted him as well. Then Profane, after bowing to them all, said, “Let Mansoul be given to my lord Diabolus, and let him be her king forever.” And at that the hollow belly and yawning throat of hell gave so loud and hideous a groan (for that is the music of that place) that it made the mountains around it totter as if they would fall to pieces.
When they had read and considered the letter, they consulted on what answer to send back, and Lucifer was the first to speak.

“The first project of the Diabolonians in Mansoul,” he said, “is likely to be lucky and to succeed: namely, that they will make Mansoul still more vile and filthy by every way and means they can. There is no way to destroy a soul like this one. Our old friend Balaam went this way, and prospered, many years ago. Let this stand with us as a maxim, then, and be a general rule for Diabolonians in every age; for nothing can make it fail but grace, and I would hope this town has no share in that. But whether we should fall on them on a market day, because they are so taken up with business then, that I would put under debate. And there is more reason to debate this point than any other, because the whole of what we attempt will turn on it. If we do not time our business well, our whole project may fail. Our friends say a market day is best, because then Mansoul will be busiest and think least of a surprise. But what if they should double their guards on those days? (And I would think nature and reason should teach them to do it.) And what if they should keep such a watch on those days as the necessity of their present case requires? Yes, what if their men should be always under arms on those days? Then, my lords, you may be disappointed, and bring our friends in the town into danger of unavoidable ruin.”

Then the great Beelzebub said, “There is something in what my lord has said; but his guess may or may not turn out to be right. Nor has my lord laid it down as a point that must not be departed from; I know he said it only to stir up a warm debate on it. So we must find out, if we can, whether Mansoul has such a sense and knowledge of her decayed state, and of the design we have on foot against her, as to move her to set watch and guard at her gates, and to double them on market days. But if, after inquiry, it is found that they are asleep, then any day will do, though a market day is best. And this is my judgment in this case.”
“How are we to know this?” said Diabolus.
“Ask Mr. Profane,” came the answer. So Profane was called in and asked the question, and he answered as follows:

“My lords, as far as I can gather, this is the present condition of Mansoul. They have declined in their faith and love. Emmanuel their Prince has turned his back on them. They often send petitions to bring him back, but he makes no haste to answer their request; nor is there much reformation among them.”

“I am glad they are slow to reform,” said Diabolus, “but still I am afraid of their petitioning. However, their loose way of living is a sign that there is not much heart in what they do; and without the heart, things are worth little. But go on, my masters; I will not distract you any longer, my lords.”
“If the case with Mansoul is as Mr. Profane has described it,” said Beelzebub, “it will make no great difference what day we assault it. Neither their prayers nor their power will do them much good.”

When Beelzebub had finished his speech, Apollyon began. “My opinion on this matter,” he said, “is that we go on gently and slowly, not doing things in a hurry. Let our friends in Mansoul keep on polluting and defiling it by trying to draw it still further into sin; for there is nothing like sin to devour Mansoul. If this is done and takes effect, Mansoul will of herself give up watching, petitioning, and everything else that makes for her security and safety. For she will forget her Emmanuel, she will not desire his company; and if she can be brought to live like this, her Prince will not be quick to come to her. Our trusty friend Mr. Carnal-Security drove him out of the town with one of his tricks; and why may not my Lord Covetousness and my Lord Lasciviousness keep him out by what they can do? And I will tell you this (not because you do not know it): two or three Diabolonians, if they are taken in and favored by the town, will do more to keep Emmanuel away from them, and to make Mansoul your own, than an army of a legion sent out from us to oppose him.

“So let this first project that our friends in Mansoul have set on foot be carried on strongly and diligently, with all the cunning and craft imaginable; and let them keep sending more of their men, under one disguise or another, to play with the people of Mansoul. Then perhaps we will not need to go to the expense of making war on them at all; or if we must, still, the more sinful they are, the less able, you may be sure, they will be to resist us, and the more easily we will overcome them. And besides, suppose (and this is the worst that can be supposed) that Emmanuel should come back to them again: why may not the same means, or something like them, drive him away from them once more? Yes, why may he not be driven from them forever by their falling back into that very sin for which he was driven away from them for a season at first? And if that should happen, then away with him go his rams, his slings, his captains, and his soldiers, and he leaves Mansoul naked and bare. Yes, when this town sees herself utterly forsaken by her Prince, will she not open her gates to you again of her own accord, and make much of you as in the old days? But this must be done over time. A few days will not accomplish so great a work as this.”

As soon as Apollyon had finished speaking, Diabolus began to blow off his own malice and plead his own cause. “My lords, and powers of the cave, my true and trusty friends,” he said, “I have listened to your long and tedious speeches with as much impatience as becomes me. But my furious throat and empty belly so lust after repossessing my famous town of Mansoul that, whatever comes of it, I can wait no longer to see how lingering projects turn out. I must, and without further delay, try by every means I can to fill my bottomless gulf with the soul and body of Mansoul. So lend me your heads, your hearts, and your help, now that I am going to recover my town of Mansoul.”

When the lords and princes of the pit saw the burning desire in Diabolus to devour the miserable town of Mansoul, they stopped raising objections and agreed to lend him what strength they could; though if Apollyon’s advice had been taken, they would have distressed Mansoul far more fearfully. They were willing, I say, not knowing what need they might have of him when they came to fight for themselves, as he did now. So they went on to discuss the next thing proposed: namely, what soldiers, and how many, Diabolus should take with him to capture Mansoul. After some debate it was concluded, just as the Diabolonians had suggested in their letter, that none were fitter for that expedition than an army of terrible Doubters. The number judged fit for that service was between twenty and thirty thousand.

So the result of that great council of high and mighty lords was this: that Diabolus should at once beat his drum for recruits in the land of Doubting, which lies on the borders of the place called Hell-Gate Hill, for men to use against the miserable town. It was also concluded that these lords themselves would help him in the war, and to that end would lead and command his men. So they drew up a letter and sent it back to the Diabolonians lurking in Mansoul, who were waiting for Mr. Profane’s return, to tell them what shape the design had now taken and how far it had come. Its contents now follow:

From the dark and horrible dungeon of hell, Diabolus, with all the fellowship of the princes of darkness, sends to our trusty ones in and around the walls of the town of Mansoul, now impatiently waiting for our most devilish answer to their venomous and most poisonous design against the town of Mansoul:

Our native ones, in whom we boast from day to day, and in whose doings we take great delight all year long: we received your welcome letter, welcome because so highly prized, at the hand of our trusty and greatly beloved old gentleman, Mr. Profane. And we would have you know that when we had opened it and read its contents, our yawning, hollow-bellied place where we live (be it said to your everlasting fame) made so hideous and yelling a noise for joy that the mountains standing round about Hell-Gate Hill were nearly shaken to pieces at the sound.

We could do no less, too, than marvel at your faithfulness to us, and at the great subtlety that has now shown itself in your heads to serve us against Mansoul. For you have devised so excellent a method for our proceedings against that rebellious people that all the wits of hell could not think of a more effective one. Since we saw the proposals you have now at last sent us, we have done little else but approve and admire them.

Indeed, to encourage you in the depth of your craft, we will let you know that at a full assembly and conclave of the princes and principalities of this place, your project was discussed and tossed from one side of our cave to the other by their mightinesses; but with all their wits they could not invent a better, or (as they themselves judged) a more fit and proper way to surprise, take, and make our own the rebellious town of Mansoul.

In short, then, everything said that differed from what you proposed in your letter fell to the ground of itself, and Diabolus the prince stuck to yours alone; yes, his gaping throat and yawning belly were on fire to put your invention into practice.

We therefore let you know that our stout, furious, and merciless Diabolus is raising, for your relief and the ruin of that rebellious town, more than twenty thousand Doubters to come against its people. They are all stout and sturdy men, long accustomed to war, who can therefore well endure the drum. I say, he is doing this work of his with all possible speed, for his heart and spirit are set on it. We desire, therefore, that as you have stood by us and given us advice and encouragement so far, you will still carry on our design. You will not lose by it, but gain; for we intend to make you the lords of Mansoul.

One thing must not on any account be left out. Those of us here desire that every one of you in Mansoul would still use all your power, cunning, and skill, with deceiving persuasions, to draw Mansoul into more sin and wickedness, so that sin, once it is full-grown, may give birth to death. [James 1:15]

For this is what we have concluded: the more vile, sinful, and debauched the town of Mansoul is, the slower their Emmanuel will be to come to their help, whether in person or by any other relief. Yes, the more sinful they are, the weaker they will be, and so the less able to resist when we make our assault on them to swallow them up. Yes, it may even cause their mighty Shaddai himself to cast them out of his protection, and to send for his captains and soldiers to come home, with his slings and rams, and leave them naked and bare; and then Mansoul will open to us of itself, and fall like the ripe fig into the mouth of the eater. Yes, you may be sure that then we will come upon her and overcome her with a great deal of ease.

As to the time of our coming against Mansoul, we have not yet fully settled it, though some of us at present think as you do, that a market day, or a market day at night, will certainly be best. In any case, be ready; and when you hear our roaring drum outside, be just as busy making the most horrible confusion inside. So Mansoul will certainly be harassed in front and behind, and will not know which way to turn for help. My Lord Lucifer, my Lord Beelzebub, my Lord Apollyon, my Lord Legion, and the rest send you their greetings, as does my Lord Diabolus; and we wish you, with all that you do or will possess, the very same fruit and success for your doings as we ourselves at present enjoy for ours.
From our dreadful borders in the most fearful pit we greet you, and so do the many legions here with us, wishing you may be as hellishly prosperous as we wish to be ourselves.
By the letter-carrier, Mr. Profane.

Then Mr. Profane set out for Mansoul with his errand from the horrible pit. He came up the stairs from the deep to the mouth of the cave, where Cerberus was; and Cerberus asked him how matters were going below against the town of Mansoul.

“Things are going as well as we could expect,” said Profane. “The letter I carried down was highly approved by all my lords, and I am going back to tell our Diabolonians so. I have an answer to it here inside my coat that I am sure will make our masters who sent me glad; for its contents encourage them to pursue their design to the utmost, and to be ready to fall on from within when they see my Lord Diabolus besieging Mansoul.”
“But does he intend to go against them himself?”
“Does he! Yes, and he will take with him more than twenty thousand, all sturdy Doubters and men of war, picked men from the land of Doubting, to serve him in the expedition.”

Then Cerberus was glad. “And are such fine preparations being made to go against the miserable town of Mansoul?” he said. “I wish I might be put at the head of a thousand of them, so that I too might show my courage against the famous town of Mansoul.”
“Your wish may come true,” said Profane. “You look like someone with plenty of mettle, and my lord will have with him those who are bold and stout. But my business requires haste.”

“Yes, so it does,” said Cerberus. “Hurry to the town of Mansoul, with all the deepest mischiefs this place can give you. And when you come to the house of Mr. Mischief, where the Diabolonians meet to plot, tell them that Cerberus sends them his service, and that if he can, he will come up with the army against the famous town of Mansoul.”
“That I will. And I know my lords there will be glad to hear it, and to see you too.”

After a few more compliments of this sort, Mr. Profane took his leave of his friend Cerberus; and Cerberus in turn, with a thousand of their pit-wishes, told him to hurry with all speed to his masters. At that he bowed low and took to his heels.

So he came back to Mansoul and, going as before to the house of Mr. Mischief, found the Diabolonians assembled and waiting for him. He presented himself, delivered his letter, and added this compliment: “My lords, from the borders of the pit, the high and mighty principalities and powers of the den greet you, the true Diabolonians of Mansoul, wishing you always the most fitting of their blessings, for the great service, high attempts, and brave achievements you have undertaken to restore the famous town of Mansoul to our prince Diabolus.”

This, then, was the present state of the miserable town of Mansoul: she had offended her Prince, and he was gone; and by her foolishness she had encouraged the powers of hell to come against her and seek her utter destruction.

It is true that Mansoul had been made somewhat aware of her sin; but the Diabolonians had got into her very bowels. She cried, but Emmanuel was gone, and her cries had not yet brought him back. Besides, she did not know now whether he would ever return and come to his Mansoul again. Nor did they know the power and diligence of the enemy, or how eager they were to carry out the plot of hell they had devised against her.

They did indeed still send petition after petition to the Prince, but he answered them all with silence. They neglected reformation, and that was just as Diabolus wanted it; for he knew that if they cherished iniquity in their heart, their King would not hear their prayer. [Ps. 66:18] So they grew weaker and weaker still, and were like whirling dust before the storm. They cried to their King for help, and kept Diabolonians in their bosoms: what, then, should a King do with them? Yes, there seemed now to be a mixture in Mansoul; the Diabolonians and the Mansoulians would walk the streets together. Indeed, the townspeople began to seek peace with them; for they thought that, since the sickness had been so deadly in Mansoul, it was useless to come to grips with them. Besides, the weakness of Mansoul was the strength of her enemies, and the sins of Mansoul the advantage of the Diabolonians. The foes of Mansoul now began to count on having the town for their own possession. There was no great difference now between Mansoulians and Diabolonians; both seemed to be masters of Mansoul. Yes, the Diabolonians increased and grew, but Mansoul dwindled greatly. More than eleven thousand men, women, and children died of the sickness in Mansoul.
